title: The Life Of A T-Shirt Activity

description.x: The clothing industry is the 3rd largest industry in the world, after cars and technology, and clothes are bought and thrown away faster than at any point in history — the United Kingdom, where this activity was written, buys more per person than any other country in Europe.1 All of it has a price. The global textiles, clothing and footwear industries have a greater effect on the environment than aviation and shipping put together.2 In this game young people put the eight stages of making a cotton t-shirt into order, from field to landfill, and then rank each stage by the carbon it emits and the water it uses. The activity is built on the evidence in the Quantis (2018) report 'Measuring Fashion: Insights from the Environmental Impact of the Global Apparel and Footwear Industries'.3

objective.x: Young people match the name of each stage in the life of a t-shirt with the industrial process it involves, and understand what actually happens at each one.
They see that even a cheap, simple garment has a long and complicated supply chain, with an environmental cost at every link in it.
They rank each stage by the carbon it emits and the water it uses — and find out where they guessed wrong.

discussion.x: MATERIALS: 8 production stage Title cards; 8 production stage Description cards; 8 Carbon emission ranking cards, numbered 1 to 8 (red); 8 Use of water ranking cards, numbered 1 to 8 (blue); 8 Cotton clue cards. QUESTIONS: Before you start — how many separate stages do you think there are in making a t-shirt? Do you think making a t-shirt has a small, medium or large environmental impact, and why? Afterwards — what do you conclude? And where in that chain could the life of a t-shirt actually be made less damaging?

sequence.x: Cut out the Life of a t-shirt Title cards and mix them up.
Cut out the Life of a t-shirt Description cards and mix them up.
Cut out the Carbon emission ranking cards and put them in a pile, 1 to 8.
Cut out the Use of water ranking cards and put them in a pile, 1 to 8.
Young people match each Title card with its Description card. The correct answers are below.

Now the Carbon emission ranking cards. Using their own judgement, they place card 1 next to the stage they think emits the most carbon, card 2 next to the second greatest, and so on down to card 8. The correct answers are below.
Same again with the Use of water ranking cards: card 1 next to the stage they think uses the most water, down to card 8. The correct answers are below.
The Cotton clue cards give clues to both rankings. Warn the group first: the clues are not all equally relevant, and some will lead a confident group straight to the wrong answer.
When the activity is finished, check the answers. Ask what surprised them and where the group disagreed. Then draw the conclusions.

content_note: The global figures here are from the Quantis 2018 report this session names, and they hold anywhere. The clothing-disposal figure on the clue cards is Britain's and is labelled as such — no Indian number has been substituted, because none is published in this document or on this site. Note also that the CLUE CARDS themselves were a table in the source document and its columns were flattened into a single run of text on extraction, so print them from the original rather than from this page. What the game teaches — the eight stages of making a cotton t-shirt, and ranking them by water and carbon — is the same in any country. The OUTCOMES and MATERIALS lists were printed in two columns and were interleaved line by line on extraction; Swechha has separated them back out, which changes their wording but not what they ask for.
